course.title: Model Thinking
course.description: A practical tour of the formal models that help you reason about a messy world - from decision trees and tipping points to networks, markets, and collective action - so you can be a many-model thinker instead of a one-story thinker. Structure adapted from University of Michigan open courseware (open.umich.edu, CC BY 3.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The main argument for being a 'many-model thinker' is that...
options: one perfect model beats several rough ones
many rough models together catch errors and cover more of reality than any single model
more data always removes the need for models
questions.explanation: Different models highlight different forces; used together they reduce blind spots - see 'Why model: the many-model thinker'.

questions.prompt: The expected value of a bet that pays 100 with probability 0.3 and 0 otherwise is...
questions.explanation: Expected value = 0.3 x 100 + 0.7 x 0 = 30 - see 'Decision models'.

questions.prompt: A 'tipping point' in a model is best described as...
options: a threshold where a small change flips the system into a very different state
a random shock with no lasting effect
questions.explanation: Below the threshold little happens; cross it and the system cascades - see 'Tipping points and thresholds'.

questions.prompt: In a social network, a person who connects otherwise separate groups sits in a...
questions.explanation: Bridges spanning structural holes carry novel information between clusters - see 'Network models'.

questions.prompt: In the simple contagion (SIR) picture, an outbreak grows when each infected person infects on average...
questions.explanation: If the reproduction number exceeds 1, cases multiply; below 1 they die out - see 'Diffusion and contagion'.

questions.prompt: If demand rises and supply is unchanged, the standard market model predicts the equilibrium price will...
questions.explanation: More buyers competing for the same quantity bid the clearing price up - see 'Economic models'.

questions.prompt: A 'collective action problem' occurs when...
options: everyone's private incentive leads to an outcome worse for all than cooperating
there is no conflict of interest at all
questions.explanation: Each person free-rides rationally, yet the group ends up worse off - see 'Game-theoretic thinking'.

questions.prompt: 'Path dependence' means that...
options: outcomes depend only on today's conditions
the order and history of past events shape which outcome you end up locked into
every path leads to the same place
questions.explanation: Early events and feedback can lock in an outcome that later events cannot easily undo - see 'Path dependence and feedback'.

lessons.title: Why model: the many-model thinker
lessons.grammar_note: A model is a deliberate simplification: you strip away detail on purpose so the few forces that matter become visible and testable.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a formal model is, list concrete reasons to build one, and argue why keeping several models beats trusting a single story. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, why might three rough models be safer than one polished one?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A model is a simplified, explicit description of how something works, usually with named parts and rules that connect them. You give up realism on purpose so you can reason clearly, compute consequences, and test predictions against data. Models help you in several ways: they force your assumptions into the open, they let you deduce results you could not see by intuition alone, they let you run experiments that would be impossible in the real world, and they travel across domains so one structure explains many situations. The many-model thinker keeps a collection of these lenses. No single model is right, but each captures one force, and combining them cancels individual errors much the way averaging many rough measurements lands near the truth. When several different models point at the same conclusion, you should trust it more; when they disagree, they have told you exactly where the uncertainty lives.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Consider explaining why a new coffee shop thrives. A market model points to price and local demand. A network model points to word of mouth spreading along friendships. A tipping model points to a threshold: once enough regulars appear, the place feels busy and attracts more. Each alone is incomplete; together they explain more. A numeric taste of the wisdom of combining: suppose three analysts estimate next-quarter sales as 90, 110, and 130, and the truth turns out to be 100. Their errors are minus 10, plus 10, and plus 30, so individually they are off by 10, 10, and 30. But their average is (90 + 110 + 130) / 3 = 110, off by only 10 - and if their high and low guesses had straddled 100 more evenly, the average would beat every one of them. Diverse models behave like diverse estimators.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Give one reason a model can be useful even when it is not fully realistic. 2) Two forecasters guess 80 and 120; the truth is 100. What is the average error of the two guesses, and what is the error of their average? 3) Name two different models you might use to explain why a rumor spread through an office. 4) True or false: a good model includes every detail of the real system. 5) If four models all predict the same direction of change, should your confidence go up or down? Answers: 1) It clarifies assumptions and lets you deduce consequences and test them. 2) Each guess is off by 20, so the average error is 20; their average is 100, off by 0. 3) For example a contagion model and a network model. 4) False - a model deliberately leaves detail out. 5) Up: agreement across different lenses is stronger evidence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: judging a model by how realistic it looks rather than by what it helps you predict or understand. Mistake: falling in love with one model and forcing every problem through it. Exit: (a) State one concrete benefit of building a model. (b) Why does averaging several diverse models tend to beat any single one? Answers: it makes assumptions explicit and lets you deduce and test consequences; because their independent errors partly cancel.

lessons.title: Categorization and linear models
lessons.grammar_note: A linear model just adds up weighted parts: outcome = base + w1 times x1 + w2 times x2 + ... Each weight says how much one input moves the result.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sort cases into meaningful categories, read the weights in a simple linear model, and use the model to predict an outcome from its inputs. Warm-up: if every extra year of experience adds about 2,000 to a salary, how much do five years add?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Two of the most useful everyday models are categorization and the linear model. Categorization groups cases so that members of a group behave alike; a good categorization has low variation inside each group and clear differences between groups, which is why splitting customers into a few sensible segments explains behavior better than treating everyone as identical or as unique. The linear model goes further and assigns each input a weight, then predicts an outcome by adding the weighted inputs to a baseline. The sign of a weight tells you direction, and its size tells you how strongly that input matters, holding the others fixed. Linear models are popular because they are transparent, they combine many factors cleanly, and they often predict surprisingly well even when the true relationship is only roughly straight.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Suppose a simple model predicts a used-car price as price = 20000 - 1500 x (age in years) - 0.05 x (miles driven). A three-year-old car with 40,000 miles is predicted at 20000 - 1500 x 3 - 0.05 x 40000 = 20000 - 4500 - 2000 = 13500. Reading the weights: each year of age subtracts 1,500, and every 10,000 miles subtracts 0.05 x 10000 = 500. Categorization example: split 6 shops into two groups by location. Downtown shops have daily sales 100, 120, 110 (average 110); suburb shops have 60, 70, 50 (average 60). Within each group sales cluster tightly, but the group averages differ by 50 - the categorization captures a real pattern that a single overall average of about 85 would hide.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Using price = 20000 - 1500 x age - 0.05 x miles, predict the price of a 5-year-old car with 60,000 miles. 2) In that model, what does the weight -1500 mean? 3) A tip model says tip = 2 + 0.15 x bill. What tip does a 40 bill predict? 4) Group A values are 8, 9, 10 and group B values are 2, 3, 4. What are the two group averages? 5) Why is a categorization with low within-group variation useful? Answers: 1) 20000 - 7500 - 3000 = 9500. 2) Each additional year of age lowers the predicted price by 1,500, holding miles fixed. 3) 2 + 0.15 x 40 = 2 + 6 = 8. 4) 9 and 3. 5) Because members of a group behave alike, so the group label predicts behavior well.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a weight as a cause rather than as an association that holds the other inputs fixed. Mistake: making so many tiny categories that each holds almost no cases and the pattern disappears into noise. Exit: (a) In outcome = base + w x input, what does the sign of w tell you? (b) What makes a categorization good? Answers: the direction of the effect (positive raises the outcome, negative lowers it); low variation within groups and clear differences between them.

lessons.title: Decision models: expected value and decision trees
lessons.grammar_note: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability: EV = sum of (probability of an outcome times its payoff). Probabilities of all outcomes must add to 1.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute the expected value of a risky choice and use a decision tree to pick the branch with the best expected payoff. Warm-up: a coin flip pays 10 on heads and 0 on tails - what is the average payoff over many flips?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When outcomes are uncertain, a decision model helps you choose without pretending you know the future. The core tool is expected value: multiply each possible payoff by its probability and add them up. It is the long-run average payoff if you faced the same gamble many times. A decision tree lays a sequence of choices and chance events out visually: square nodes are your decisions, circular nodes are chance events with branches that carry probabilities, and the tips carry payoffs. You solve a tree by 'folding back' from right to left - compute the expected value at each chance node, then at each decision node keep the branch with the highest value. This turns a tangled choice into simple arithmetic. Expected value is not the whole story when a loss could ruin you, but it is the right starting point and the benchmark every other rule is measured against.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A stall costs 50 to run for the day. If the weather is good (probability 0.6) you earn 200; if it is bad (probability 0.4) you earn 20. Expected revenue = 0.6 x 200 + 0.4 x 20 = 120 + 8 = 128, so expected profit = 128 - 50 = 78, which is positive, so running the stall beats the 0 payoff of staying home. Now a decision tree with two products. Product A: launch cost aside, it yields 100 with probability 0.5 and 40 with probability 0.5, so EV = 0.5 x 100 + 0.5 x 40 = 70. Product B yields 200 with probability 0.3 and 0 with probability 0.7, so EV = 0.3 x 200 = 60. Folding back at the decision node, you choose Product A because 70 is greater than 60 - even though B has the bigger possible prize.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A ticket pays 500 with probability 0.02 and 0 otherwise. What is its expected value? 2) Would you pay 15 for that ticket on expected value alone? 3) Option X: 0.5 chance of 80 and 0.5 chance of 20 - what is its EV? 4) Option Y gives a sure 55. On expected value, which do you pick, X or Y? 5) In a decision tree, what do you do at a chance node versus a decision node? Answers: 1) 0.02 x 500 = 10. 2) No - paying 15 for an expected 10 loses 5 on average. 3) 0.5 x 80 + 0.5 x 20 = 40 + 10 = 50. 4) Y, since a sure 55 beats an expected 50. 5) At a chance node you take the probability-weighted average of its branches; at a decision node you keep the branch with the highest value.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: comparing options by their best possible outcome instead of their expected value. Mistake: letting probabilities that do not sum to 1 slip into the calculation. Exit: (a) Write the expected value of 'win 90 with probability 0.2, else 0.' (b) When solving a decision tree, in which direction do you fold back? Answers: 0.2 x 90 = 18; from the payoffs on the right back toward the first decision on the left.

questions.prompt: The strongest reason to keep several models rather than one is that...
options: diverse models' errors partly cancel and cover more forces
models with more detail are always better
questions.explanation: Combining diverse lenses reduces blind spots and averages out individual errors.

questions.prompt: In price = 20000 - 1500 x age - 0.05 x miles, a 2-year-old car with 20,000 miles is predicted at...
The expected value of 'win 100 with probability 0.3, win 0 otherwise' is...
Option X has EV 70 and Option Y is a sure 65. On expected value you should...
questions.explanation: 70 is greater than 65, so X wins on expected value.

questions.prompt: A good categorization of cases has...
options: low variation inside groups and clear differences between them
questions.explanation: Tight groups that differ from each other let the label predict behavior.

questions.prompt: When solving a decision tree, at a chance node you...
options: take the probability-weighted average of its branches
questions.explanation: Chance nodes are averaged by probability; decision nodes take the max.

lessons.title: Tipping points and thresholds
lessons.grammar_note: A threshold model gives each actor a trigger point: they switch behavior only once the share of others already switched passes their personal threshold.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Spot a tipping point, use a threshold rule to trace whether a change spreads or stalls, and explain why tiny differences in starting conditions can flip the outcome. Warm-up: if you would only join a protest once 30 percent of your neighbors already had, what is your threshold?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Some systems change smoothly, but many have a tipping point: a threshold where a small nudge flips the system into a very different state, and it does not simply flip back. A clean way to model this is with individual thresholds. Each person adopts a behavior only when the fraction of others who already adopted exceeds their own threshold. Line the thresholds up and you can trace a cascade step by step: the lowest-threshold people go first, their action raises the adopted fraction, which trips the next people, and so on - or the chain stalls if there is a gap no one bridges. Because the cascade depends on the exact spread of thresholds, two nearly identical crowds can behave completely differently, which is the signature of a tipping system.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Five people have thresholds 0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.60, 0.90, measured as the fraction of the other four who must already act. Start: the person with threshold 0 acts with no prompting, so 1 of 5 = 0.20 have acted. That 0.20 exceeds the 0.10 threshold, so the second person acts; now 2 of 5 = 0.40 have acted. That trips the 0.30 person: 3 of 5 = 0.60 have acted. That exactly reaches the 0.60 person, who acts: 4 of 5 = 0.80. But the last threshold is 0.90, which 0.80 does not reach, so the cascade stops at four adopters. Now change one number: raise the second threshold from 0.10 to 0.25. After the first actor, 0.20 no longer clears 0.25, so nobody else moves and the cascade dies at one adopter. A tiny change in one threshold took the outcome from four adopters to one.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Thresholds are 0, 0.20, 0.40 among three people (fraction of the other two). Does the first actor's 1 of 3 = 0.33 trip the 0.20 person? 2) Continue: after two have acted, 2 of 3 = 0.67 - does that trip the 0.40 person? 3) What is the final number of adopters? 4) In one phrase, what defines a tipping point? 5) Why can two similar groups tip differently? Answers: 1) Yes, 0.33 exceeds 0.20 so the second person acts. 2) Yes, 0.67 exceeds 0.40, so the third acts. 3) All three adopt. 4) A threshold where a small change flips the system into a very different state. 5) Because the cascade depends on the exact arrangement of thresholds, so small differences change everything.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming change is always gradual and proportional to the push. Mistake: forgetting to recompute the adopted fraction after each new adopter before checking the next threshold. Exit: (a) In a threshold model, when does a person switch? (b) Why are tipping systems hard to predict? Answers: when the fraction of others already switched passes their personal threshold; because outcomes hinge on small details of the starting conditions.

lessons.title: Network models
lessons.grammar_note: In a network, degree is how many connections a node has; a path length is the number of edges you cross to get from one node to another. Short paths mean fast spread.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe a network by its nodes and edges, compute a node's degree, and explain why bridges and short paths matter for how things spread. Warm-up: in a group chat of 6 people all connected to each other, how many people is any one person connected to?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A network is a set of nodes joined by edges: people and friendships, airports and flights, computers and cables. Two simple measures carry a lot of weight. A node's degree is its number of edges, and highly connected hubs exert outsized influence on flow. Path length is the number of edges between two nodes; when typical paths are short, information, disease, or money travels fast across the whole system, the famous 'small world' effect. A third idea is the bridge: an edge that connects two otherwise separate clusters spans a structural hole and carries novel information, because everything inside a tight cluster tends to be already shared. Networks matter because outcomes often depend less on individual traits and more on who is connected to whom.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Take 6 people in a fully connected group: each person has degree 5, since they link to the other five, and the total number of edges is C(6, 2) = 6 x 5 / 2 = 15. Now a line of 5 people A-B-C-D-E: the endpoints A and E have degree 1, the middle three have degree 2, and the path length from A to E is 4 edges. Add one bridge edge from A to E and that longest path drops from 4 to 1, dramatically shortening distances across the whole line. Hub example: in a star with one center connected to 5 others, the center has degree 5 while each outer node has degree 1, so removing the center disconnects everyone - a vivid illustration of how much a single hub can matter.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In a fully connected group of 4, what is each node's degree? 2) How many edges does that group have? 3) In the line A-B-C-D, what is the path length from A to D? 4) Which node matters most in a star network, and why? 5) What makes a bridge edge valuable? Answers: 1) Degree 3, linking to the other three. 2) C(4, 2) = 6 edges. 3) 3 edges. 4) The center, because every path runs through it and removing it disconnects the network. 5) It connects separate clusters and so carries information not already shared inside either one.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: judging influence by a person's own traits while ignoring their position in the network. Mistake: assuming a well-connected-looking graph has short paths when a missing bridge can leave clusters far apart. Exit: (a) What is a node's degree? (b) Why do short average path lengths matter? Answers: the number of edges connected to it; because they let information or contagion spread quickly across the whole network.

lessons.title: Diffusion and contagion: SIR intuition
lessons.grammar_note: In the SIR model everyone is Susceptible, Infected, or Recovered. The reproduction number R0 is the average number of new cases one infected person causes in a fully susceptible population.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the S, I, and R compartments, use the reproduction number to say whether something spreads or fades, and apply the same logic to ideas and products, not just disease. Warm-up: if each infected person passes a cold to two others on average, will cases grow or shrink at first?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Diffusion models describe how something spreads through a population. The workhorse is the SIR model, which splits everyone into three compartments: Susceptible (can catch it), Infected (has it and can pass it on), and Recovered (had it and is now immune or done). People flow S to I to R over time. The single most important number is the basic reproduction number R0: the average number of new cases one infected person generates while infectious in a fully susceptible population. If R0 is greater than 1, each case more than replaces itself and the thing spreads; if R0 is less than 1, it fades out. The same structure models product adoption and rumors, where 'infection' is trying the product and 'recovery' is losing interest - which is why a hot trend can take off and then burn out as the susceptible pool shrinks.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Start with 1 infected person in a large susceptible crowd. If R0 = 2, then early on cases roughly double each generation: 1, then 2, then 4, then 8, then 16 - clearly an outbreak. If instead R0 = 0.5, cases roughly halve each generation: 1, then on average 0.5, then 0.25 - it dies out fast. R0 also sets a rough herd-immunity share: if a fraction 1 - 1/R0 of people are already immune, each case meets on average fewer than one susceptible person and spread stalls. For R0 = 2 that fraction is 1 - 1/2 = 0.5, so immunity in about half the population halts it; for R0 = 4 it is 1 - 1/4 = 0.75. Product version: if each happy user brings in 1.3 new users on average, adoption grows; if a saturated market drops that to 0.8, growth reverses.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) With R0 = 3 starting from 1 case, roughly how many cases after two more generations? 2) Does R0 = 0.9 lead to growth or fade-out? 3) What immune fraction roughly halts spread when R0 = 4? 4) Name the three SIR compartments. 5) In a product-adoption version, what plays the role of 'infected'? Answers: 1) About 1, then 3, then 9. 2) Fade-out, since it is below 1. 3) 1 - 1/4 = 0.75, about three-quarters. 4) Susceptible, Infected, Recovered. 5) A current active user who is spreading the product to others.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating R0 as fixed forever, when it falls as the susceptible pool shrinks and as behavior changes. Mistake: assuming any spread continues indefinitely, ignoring that recovery and saturation eventually starve it. Exit: (a) What does R0 greater than 1 imply? (b) What immune fraction stalls spread for R0 = 2? Answers: each case more than replaces itself, so it spreads; 1 - 1/2 = 0.5, about half.

questions.prompt: In a threshold cascade with thresholds 0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.60, 0.90 among five people, the cascade stops after...
questions.explanation: It reaches 0.80 adopted (four people) but cannot clear the 0.90 threshold.

questions.prompt: In a fully connected group of 6 people, each node has degree...
questions.explanation: Each person links to the other five, so degree 5; total edges are C(6,2) = 15.

questions.prompt: A bridge edge in a network is valuable because it...
options: adds a redundant link inside a cluster
connects separate clusters and carries novel information
questions.explanation: Bridges span structural holes between clusters, carrying information not already shared.

questions.prompt: If the reproduction number R0 equals 0.7, an outbreak will...
questions.explanation: R0 below 1 means each case fails to replace itself, so cases shrink.

questions.prompt: For R0 = 2, spread roughly stalls once the immune fraction reaches about...
questions.explanation: The herd-immunity share is 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/2 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: The three compartments of the SIR model are...
questions.explanation: People flow from Susceptible to Infected to Recovered.

lessons.title: Economic models: supply, demand, and market signals
lessons.grammar_note: Equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Demand slopes down (higher price, less bought); supply slopes up (higher price, more offered).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Find a market's equilibrium price and quantity, predict how a shift in supply or demand moves them, and read prices as signals that coordinate strangers. Warm-up: if a heatwave makes everyone want more ice, what happens to its price?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The supply-and-demand model explains how a price forms without anyone setting it centrally. The demand curve slopes down: as price rises, buyers want less. The supply curve slopes up: as price rises, sellers offer more. They cross at the equilibrium, the price where quantity demanded exactly equals quantity supplied and the market clears. Prices then work as signals: a high price shouts 'scarce, produce more, use less,' and a low price whispers the opposite, so millions of strangers coordinate without anyone in charge. When something shifts a whole curve, you can predict the result: an increase in demand raises both price and quantity, while an increase in supply lowers price but raises quantity. The model is a simplification, but it is astonishingly good at explaining shortages, surpluses, and why prices move the way they do.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Let quantity demanded be Qd = 100 - 2P and quantity supplied be Qs = 20 + 2P, where P is price. Set them equal: 100 - 2P = 20 + 2P, so 80 = 4P and P = 20. Plug back: Qd = 100 - 40 = 60, and Qs = 20 + 40 = 60 - they match, so equilibrium is price 20, quantity 60. Now suppose demand rises to Qd = 120 - 2P (buyers want 20 more at every price). Set 120 - 2P = 20 + 2P, so 100 = 4P and P = 25, with quantity 20 + 50 = 70. Both price and quantity rose, exactly as the model predicts for a demand increase. If instead supply had increased to Qs = 40 + 2P with the original demand, then 100 - 2P = 40 + 2P gives 60 = 4P, P = 15 and quantity 70: price fell, quantity rose.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) With Qd = 90 - 3P and Qs = 10 + P, find the equilibrium price. 2) What is the equilibrium quantity there? 3) If demand rises, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity? 4) If supply rises, what happens to price? 5) In one phrase, what does a high price signal to producers? Answers: 1) 90 - 3P = 10 + P gives 80 = 4P, so P = 20. 2) Qs = 10 + 20 = 30 (and Qd = 90 - 60 = 30). 3) Both rise. 4) Price falls (and quantity rises). 5) That the good is scarce and more should be produced.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing a shift of the whole curve with a movement along it caused by a price change. Mistake: thinking a demand increase must raise quantity but lower price - it raises both. Exit: (a) At equilibrium, what is true of quantity demanded and quantity supplied? (b) An increase in supply moves price which way? Answers: they are equal; price falls while quantity rises.

lessons.title: Game-theoretic thinking and collective action
lessons.grammar_note: In a game, a strategy is dominant if it gives a player a better payoff no matter what others do. An equilibrium is a set of strategies where no one gains by switching alone.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a simple payoff table, find a dominant strategy and an equilibrium, and explain why rational individuals can produce a group outcome everyone dislikes. Warm-up: if cutting your price wins customers whatever your rival does, will you cut it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Game theory models decisions where your best move depends on what others do. A game lists players, their possible strategies, and the payoffs for each combination. A strategy is dominant if it beats a player's other options no matter what the others choose, and a rational player uses it. An equilibrium is a stable point where no player can do better by changing alone. The famous prisoner's dilemma shows the sting of collective action problems: each player has a dominant strategy to defect, so both defect, yet both would be better off if they had cooperated. The same structure explains overfishing, price wars, and why shared resources get depleted: individually rational choices add up to a collectively bad result. Recognizing this pattern is the first step to fixing it, usually by changing the payoffs through agreements, repetition, or rules.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Two firms each choose High price or Low price. If both go High, each earns 10. If both go Low, each earns 5. If one goes Low while the other stays High, the low-priced firm grabs the market for 12 and the high-priced firm gets 2. Check Firm 1's best response: if Firm 2 plays High, Firm 1 earns 10 by High or 12 by Low, so Low is better; if Firm 2 plays Low, Firm 1 earns 2 by High or 5 by Low, so Low is better again. Low is dominant for both, so both play Low and each earns 5 - even though both playing High would have paid 10 each. That gap, 5 versus 10, is the collective action problem in numbers. A cooperation fix: if the firms interact repeatedly and each punishes a price cut next round, the long-run value of staying High can exceed the one-time gain from cutting, and cooperation becomes sustainable.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In the game above, what does Firm 1 earn if it plays Low while Firm 2 plays High? 2) Is High or Low the dominant strategy? 3) What does each firm earn at the equilibrium? 4) What would each earn if both cooperated on High? 5) Name one mechanism that can help players escape the dilemma. Answers: 1) 12. 2) Low, because it beats High whatever the rival does. 3) 5 each. 4) 10 each. 5) Repetition with punishment for defection (also binding agreements or outside rules).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming that because cooperation is best for the group, rational players will choose it. Mistake: reading only your own payoffs and forgetting the move depends on the other player's choice. Exit: (a) What makes a strategy dominant? (b) Why is the prisoner's dilemma called a collective action problem? Answers: it yields a higher payoff regardless of what others do; because each person's rational choice leads to an outcome worse for all than cooperating.

lessons.title: Aggregation: the wisdom and madness of crowds
lessons.grammar_note: The diversity-prediction result: a crowd's squared error = the average member's squared error minus the diversity of their predictions. More diversity means a smarter crowd.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain when averaging many independent guesses beats the experts, compute a simple crowd average, and say when crowds turn foolish instead. Warm-up: if three people guess a jar holds 200, 400, and 600 jellybeans, what is the crowd's guess?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Aggregation models study what happens when you combine many individual pieces into a collective outcome. A striking result is the wisdom of crowds: the average of many independent, diverse guesses is often more accurate than almost any individual, because errors in different directions cancel. This is captured by the diversity-prediction theorem, which says the crowd's error equals the average individual's error minus the crowd's diversity, so a crowd gets smarter both when its members are individually better and when they are more diverse. But the same machinery can produce madness: when people copy each other instead of guessing independently, diversity collapses, errors reinforce rather than cancel, and you get bubbles, panics, and fads. So crowds are wise when guesses are independent and diverse, and foolish when everyone imitates the same signal.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Three independent guesses for a jar are 200, 400, and 600, and the truth is 400. The crowd average is (200 + 400 + 600) / 3 = 400, exactly right, even though two of the three individuals were off by 200. Let's verify the theorem with squared errors. Individual squared errors are (200-400)^2 = 40000, (400-400)^2 = 0, and (600-400)^2 = 40000, averaging (40000 + 0 + 40000) / 3 = 26667 roughly. Diversity is the average squared distance from the crowd mean of 400, which is the same (40000 + 0 + 40000) / 3 = 26667. Crowd error = average individual error minus diversity = 26667 - 26667 = 0, matching the perfect crowd guess. Now the madness case: if the second and third people simply copy the first person's 200, all three say 200, the average is 200, diversity is 0, and the crowd is off by the full 200 - copying destroyed the wisdom.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Four guesses are 10, 20, 30, 40. What is the crowd average? 2) If the truth is 25, how far off is the crowd? 3) In the diversity-prediction theorem, what two things make a crowd more accurate? 4) What happens to diversity when everyone copies one person? 5) Name one real phenomenon caused by lost diversity. Answers: 1) (10 + 20 + 30 + 40) / 4 = 25. 2) It is exactly right, off by 0. 3) More accurate individuals and more diversity among them. 4) Diversity drops toward 0, so the crowd is no better than that one person. 5) A speculative bubble or a panic (also fads or herding).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing any large crowd is automatically wise, even when members are copying one another. Mistake: assuming you need expert guesses; diverse ordinary guesses can beat the experts once averaged. Exit: (a) Why does averaging independent diverse guesses work so well? (b) What turns a wise crowd into a foolish one? Answers: their errors point in different directions and cancel; loss of independence and diversity when people imitate each other.

questions.prompt: With Qd = 100 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P, the equilibrium price is...
questions.explanation: 100 - 2P = 20 + 2P gives 80 = 4P, so P = 20, with quantity 60.

questions.prompt: An increase in demand, supply unchanged, moves equilibrium price and quantity...
questions.explanation: More buyers at every price bid up the price and clear a larger quantity.

questions.prompt: In the price-setting game where Low earns 12 against High but both-Low earns 5 each, the equilibrium is...
questions.explanation: Low is dominant for both, so both play Low and earn 5 each, below the 10 of mutual cooperation.

questions.prompt: A strategy that beats a player's other options no matter what others do is called...
questions.explanation: A dominant strategy is best regardless of others' choices.

questions.prompt: Guesses 200, 400, 600 average to 400, the truth. This illustrates...
options: the wisdom of crowds from canceling errors
questions.explanation: Independent errors in opposite directions cancel in the average.

questions.prompt: A wise crowd turns foolish mainly when members...
options: copy one another and lose diversity
questions.explanation: Imitation collapses diversity, so errors reinforce instead of canceling.

lessons.title: Path dependence and feedback
lessons.grammar_note: Positive feedback amplifies a change (the rich get richer); negative feedback dampens it (a thermostat). Path dependence arises when positive feedback locks in early outcomes.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell positive from negative feedback, explain how path dependence locks in an outcome, and use a simple increasing-returns process to see why history matters. Warm-up: if the next customer is more likely to pick whichever product already has more users, what happens over time?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Feedback loops shape how systems evolve over time. Negative feedback is stabilizing: it pushes a system back toward a target, the way a thermostat cuts heat as the room warms. Positive feedback is amplifying: a change feeds on itself, so small leads grow into large ones. When positive feedback is strong, you get path dependence, where the order of early events determines the final outcome and the system 'locks in' to a state that later events cannot easily reverse. This is why a technology that got an early lead can dominate even if a rival is arguably better, and why two nearly identical starts can end in different worlds. The lesson for a modeler is that in path-dependent systems, history and timing are not noise to average away; they are causes.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A classic increasing-returns process: an urn holds 1 red and 1 blue ball. You draw one, note its color, return it, and add one more ball of that same color; repeat. Each draw makes the color you just drew slightly more likely next time, which is positive feedback. Suppose early luck gives red an edge: start 1-1, draw red to make it 2-1, draw red again to make it 3-1. Red now has a 3 in 4 chance and tends to pull further ahead, and the final long-run share of red can settle anywhere depending on those first few draws - the path taken determines the destination. Contrast a negative-feedback case: if instead you added a ball of the opposite color each time, the shares would be pushed back toward balance and history would wash out. The difference between lock-in and self-correction is the sign of the feedback.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is a thermostat an example of positive or negative feedback? 2) In the urn starting 1-1, after drawing red twice (adding a red each time), what is the count of red and blue? 3) What is the chance the next draw is red then? 4) Which kind of feedback produces path dependence? 5) Give one reason a worse-but-earlier technology can dominate a better-but-later one. Answers: 1) Negative feedback, since it corrects toward a target. 2) 3 red and 1 blue. 3) 3 out of 4. 4) Positive (self-amplifying) feedback. 5) Its early lead compounds through increasing returns and locks in before the rival can catch up.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the best option always wins, ignoring how early leads lock in under positive feedback. Mistake: mixing up the two feedbacks - negative stabilizes, positive amplifies. Exit: (a) Which kind of feedback creates path dependence? (b) In a path-dependent system, why does timing matter? Answers: positive feedback; because early events amplify and lock in an outcome that later events cannot easily undo.

lessons.title: Capstone: many models on one problem
lessons.grammar_note: The many-model workflow: name the question, list which forces matter, pick the model that captures each force, run each, then combine what they say into one judgment.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Take a single real problem and attack it with several models at once, then combine their answers into a decision that no single model would give. Warm-up: which two models from this course would you reach for first to study a new app spreading on a campus?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The payoff of this course is the habit of laying several models over one problem. Each model isolates a different force; together they give a fuller, self-correcting picture. The workflow is simple: state the question sharply, list the forces you think are at play, match each force to a model you know, run each model for its own prediction, and then reconcile them into a single judgment, paying special attention to where they agree and where they clash. Agreement raises confidence; disagreement tells you exactly which assumption to check. The goal is not one grand model of everything but a small toolkit used deliberately, which is what separates a many-model thinker from someone armed with a single favorite story.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Question: should a small studio launch a new mobile game this quarter, and will it catch on? Decision model: expected value of launching. Suppose a hit (probability 0.3) nets 500 and a flop (probability 0.7) loses 100, so EV = 0.3 x 500 + 0.7 x (-100) = 150 - 70 = 80, a positive expected value, so launching beats not launching on that criterion. Contagion model: growth needs each player to recruit more than one other, so if each active player brings in about 1.4 new players, adoption should climb, but watch for saturation dropping that below 1. Network model: seed the game where clusters are dense and a few bridges connect them, so word of mouth crosses between friend groups quickly. Tipping model: there may be a threshold of visible players before the game feels 'alive,' so front-load early users to clear it. Path dependence: an early lead compounds through app-store rankings and social proof, so timing the launch to build momentum matters more than a marginally better feature set. Reconcile: all five lenses point the same way, launch and seed aggressively early, which raises confidence; the one caution they share is saturation, so the plan should monitor the recruitment ratio and act if it slips below 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In the launch example, what is the expected value of launching? 2) On expected value alone, launch or not? 3) Which model tells you to seed dense clusters connected by bridges? 4) Which model warns about a saturation point where each player recruits fewer than one other? 5) Why does agreement across all five models increase your confidence? Answers: 1) 0.3 x 500 + 0.7 x (-100) = 150 - 70 = 80. 2) Launch, since 80 is greater than 0. 3) The network model. 4) The contagion (diffusion) model. 5) Because independent lenses making the same call is stronger evidence than any one of them alone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: stopping at the first model that gives a clear answer instead of checking it against others. Mistake: treating disagreement between models as failure rather than as a map of where your uncertainty lives. Exit: (a) What are the five steps of the many-model workflow? (b) What should you do when two models disagree? Answers: state the question, list the forces, match each to a model, run each, and reconcile them; investigate the clashing assumption, because the disagreement pinpoints your key uncertainty.

models cannot be checked against data
questions.explanation: Diverse models catch each other's errors and cover more forces than one story can.

questions.explanation: Self-amplifying positive feedback lets early events lock in the result.

questions.explanation: You frame the question, map forces to models, run each, and combine their answers.
